story: Perhaps a million people at its height, the first city that size. To Han China it was the capital of Daqin, the 'great Qin' at the far end of the world.

A Phoenician colony that became the greatest power of the western Mediterranean. Rome razed it in 146 BCE after a three-year siege. A century later Caesar and Augustus founded a Roman city on the same site.
Roman Carthage, refounded on the ruins of the Punic city, grew into the second city of the western empire. It fell to the Umayyads in 698.
Founded by Alexander, home of the Library and the Pharos lighthouse, and for centuries the place where the Mediterranean met the trade of the Red Sea.

A prosperous Roman town buried under four to six metres of ash when Vesuvius erupted in 79. Pliny the Younger watched from across the bay. The town was forgotten until excavation began in 1748, nearly 1,700 years later.
Greek Byzantion, refounded by Constantine in 330 as the new capital of Rome, and from 1453 the Ottoman capital. Its names change with whoever is looking.

The Nabataean caravan city carved into rose-red cliffs. After its trade moved elsewhere it emptied, and outsiders forgot it until Johann Ludwig Burckhardt talked his way in, disguised as a pilgrim, in 1812. The local Bedouin had always known it.

A Norse camp of eight timber-and-turf buildings on the tip of Newfoundland, used for a few years around 1000. Helge and Anne Stine Ingstad found it in 1960, the first proof that Europeans reached the Americas before Columbus.

The ceremonial capital of the Persian kings. Alexander's army burned it in 330 BCE, perhaps in revenge for Athens, perhaps after a drunken feast. The ruins were never lost: local people called them Takht-e Jamshid, the throne of the legendary king Jamshid.

Built from scratch by the Abbasid caliph al-Mansur in 762 as a perfect circle of walls with the palace and mosque at its centre. Within a century it was probably the largest city in the world, and a centre of translation, mathematics and map-making.

Capital of a state that grew rich on gold traded to the Swahili coast, with curving granite walls built without mortar. It was left around 1450. Europeans who saw it from 1871 refused to believe Africans had built it; archaeology settled the question long ago.

One of the largest cities of the Bronze Age, with a grid of brick streets, drains and a great bath. When it was left around 1700 BCE even its name was lost. Archaeologists recognized what it was only in the 1920s, along with Harappa.
A Buddhist university where thousands of monks studied, Xuanzang among them. It was sacked around 1200 and forgotten until its ruins were identified in the 1860s.

Capital of the Han and the Tang, the eastern end of the Silk Road. Around 750 perhaps a million people lived inside its grid of walled wards, including merchants and monks from Persia, Sogdiana, Korea and Japan.

An oasis kingdom on the old shore of Lop Nur, a stop on the Silk Road for Chinese garrisons and caravans. As the rivers shifted and the lake dried, it was swallowed by the desert. Sven Hedin's guide stumbled on its ruins in 1900 while going back for a lost spade.
Kublai Khan's summer capital, Xanadu, described by Marco Polo. The Ming burned it in 1369. Coleridge made it a dream of luxury in 1797, long after the city had become grass-covered mounds.

The Khmer capital, a city of perhaps 750,000 spread around great reservoirs and temples. After Ayutthaya's armies sacked it in 1431 the court moved south and the forest crept in, though monks kept Angkor Wat in use. Henri Mouhot's posthumous book made it famous in Europe from the 1860s.

The Mexica capital, built on an island in Lake Texcoco and joined to the shore by causeways. In 1519 it was one of the largest cities on Earth, bigger than any in Spain. Cortés's forces and their allies destroyed it in 1521, and Mexico City was built on the ruins.

The largest city north of Mexico, around 1100 home to perhaps 10,000–20,000 people beneath a 30-metre earthen mound. By about 1350 it was empty. The mounds stayed, and later peoples and settlers saw them, but who built them was argued over for centuries.

A royal estate built for the Inca emperor Pachacuti in the mountains above the Urubamba. It was left around the time of the Spanish conquest and never found by the Spanish. Local farmers knew it well; Hiram Bingham's photographs made it known to the outside world in 1911–1913.

A great marae (sacred meeting ground) on Raʻiātea, the spiritual centre of East Polynesian voyaging. Navigators from across the region came here; stones from it were carried to found new marae on other islands.

names.name: São José da Barra do Rio Negro

story: Hadrian's city in Thrace. The Ottomans took it in 1361 and made it their capital until Constantinople fell, the base from which they crossed into the Balkans.
Iconium of Paul's journeys; from 1097 the capital of the Seljuk sultans of Rum, and the city where Rumi taught and is buried.
A Baltic island town grown rich in the Hanseatic trade, still ringed by its thirteenth-century walls and the ruins of its churches.
Phoenician, Greek, Roman, Arab and Norman in turn; under the Kalbid emirs and the Norman kings it was among the largest cities in Europe, where al-Idrisi drew his map of the world.
Charlemagne's capital, where he built his palace chapel and was buried; German kings were crowned there for six centuries.
Seat of the popes from 1309 to 1377, when the papacy left Rome for the Rhône.
A Syrian kingdom whose palace archive of some seventeen thousand clay tablets, found in 1974, revealed a forgotten language and a great power of the third millennium BCE.
Capital of the Asante, whose kings sat on the Golden Stool; British envoys in 1817 described a city of broad streets and painted houses.
The hills of the kings of Buganda, whose capitals moved from hill to hill; Speke reached Mutesa's court here in 1862.
Capital of the Funj sultanate on the Blue Nile, which ruled the middle Nile for three centuries until the Egyptian conquest of 1821.
The first European town in the tropics, on Santiago in the Cape Verde islands, and an early hub of the Atlantic slave trade.
Capital of the last Sinhalese kingdom, which held the hills against the Portuguese and Dutch and kept the Tooth Relic of the Buddha until 1815.
Capital of the Chola kings, whose great temple of 1010 crowned the empire that sent fleets to Srivijaya.
A capital drawn on an empty plateau and built in four years, to turn Brazil inward from its coast.
Capital of the state of Lu and home of Confucius, whose descendants lived beside his temple for more than two thousand years.
Capital of Qi, perhaps the largest city of the Warring States, home of the Jixia Academy where the philosophers of the age debated.
The porcelain capital, named for the Jingde reign; its blue-and-white was shipped to the Ottoman court, Persia, Africa and Europe.
Capital of Nanzhao and then the kingdom of Dali, which ruled Yunnan for five centuries until the Mongols took it in 1253.
Xingqing, capital of the Tangut Western Xia, sacked by the Mongols in 1227 as Genghis Khan lay dying.
Capital of the Ryukyu kingdom, a trading state between China, Japan, Korea and Southeast Asia until Japan annexed it in 1879.
A Tangut garrison city on the Etsin river, abandoned after the Ming cut its water in 1372; Kozlov dug thousands of Tangut books from its sand in 1908.

The tomb of the pharaoh Khufu, the tallest building on Earth for nearly four thousand years. Herodotus heard its story from priests two thousand years after it was raised, and it was already ancient to them.
A ring of great sarsens raised on Salisbury Plain, aligned with the midsummer sunrise. Its builders left no writing; by the Middle Ages it was said Merlin had flown the stones from Ireland.
Carved stone pillars raised by hunter-gatherers some seven thousand years before the pyramids, then deliberately buried. Its age was recognised only in 1994.
Ramesses II's temples cut into a Nubian cliff, facing the sunrise down the Nile. Sand buried them to the shoulders; Burckhardt glimpsed a colossal head above the dune in 1813.

Not one wall but many: for two thousand years dynasty after dynasty walled the northern frontier, each along its own line, while the walls of the last fell to ruin. The mark follows the wall of the age; the faint lines are the walls that went before.

phases.name: Warring States walls
phases.note: Rival states wall themselves off from one another and from the steppe: Qi in Shandong, Zhao, Yan and Qin in the north.

phases.name: Qin
phases.note: The First Emperor joins the northern walls into one, from Lintao to Liaodong.

phases.name: Han
phases.note: Han restores the Qin wall and carries it west along the Hexi Corridor to the Jade Gate, with beacons out toward Lop Nur, to guard the road to the West.

phases.name: Northern Qi and Sui
phases.note: Northern Qi raises a new line across Shanxi to the sea; Sui rebuilds it with forced labour.

phases.name: Tang
phases.note: With its frontier far out on the steppe, Tang builds no wall; the old ones crumble.

phases.name: Jin
phases.note: The Jurchen Jin dig border trenches behind ramparts far north across the Mongolian steppe; Genghis Khan's armies ride over them.

phases.name: Yuan
phases.note: Inside the Mongol empire the wall guards nothing and is left to ruin; only the pass at Juyongguan is adorned, with the Cloud Platform of 1345.

phases.name: Ming
phases.note: Ming rebuilds the wall from Shanhaiguan to Jiayuguan, faced in brick and stone after the 1570s: the wall seen today.

phases.name: Qing
phases.note: Once Qing armies pass Shanhaiguan in 1644 the wall is no longer a frontier, only a customs line and a slow ruin, until the twentieth century makes it a national symbol.

story: Some eight thousand clay soldiers buried to guard the First Emperor's tomb. Rebels burned the pits within a few years of his death, and they lay forgotten until farmers digging a well struck them in 1974.

The largest Buddhist monument in the world, a mountain of carved terraces in central Java. Deserted as the island's courts moved east, it vanished under ash and jungle until Raffles had it cleared in 1814.

A palace on a granite rock rising two hundred metres from the plain, with frescoed maidens painted on its face. The king who built it reigned only eighteen years; monks kept the rock for centuries after.
Buddhist halls cut into a river gorge, painted with the finest surviving murals of ancient India. Forgotten for a millennium, they were stumbled on by a British officer hunting a tiger in 1819.

Nearly a thousand stone figures carved from the crater of Rano Raraku and stood on platforms facing inland. When Roggeveen landed in 1722 many still stood; within a century and a half all had been pulled down.

Lines and figures scraped into the desert floor across hundreds of square kilometres: a hummingbird, a monkey, a spider. From the ground they are faint paths; they were first studied in 1927 and seen whole from the air.
Some five hundred painted cave temples cut into a cliff outside Dunhuang. In 1900 a monk found a sealed library of tens of thousands of manuscripts, among them the oldest dated printed book.
A sea-level canal from the Mediterranean to the Red Sea. Pharaohs and caliphs had cut canals from the Nile; this one, opened in 1869, cut the voyage from London to Bombay by nearly half.
Locks lift ships across the isthmus that Balboa crossed on foot in 1513. Its opening in 1914 ended the long passage around Cape Horn.
The Zambezi drops a hundred metres into a chasm a mile and a half wide. Its name here was Mosi-oa-Tunya, the smoke that thunders; Livingstone, shown it in 1855, named it for his queen.
A snow-capped volcano three degrees from the equator. When the missionary Rebmann reported snow on it in 1848, London geographers refused to believe him.
The Colorado River's gorge, a mile deep, home to the Havasupai. García López de Cárdenas reached the rim in 1540 and could find no way down.
A sandstone monolith in the centre of Australia, sacred to the Anangu for tens of thousands of years. William Gosse reached it in 1873 and named it Ayers Rock.
Japan's highest and most sacred mountain, a near-perfect volcanic cone last erupting in 1707. Pilgrims climbed it for centuries; Hokusai drew it thirty-six times.
The outflow of the Great Lakes pours over a broad ledge on its way to Lake Ontario. The friar Louis Hennepin, who saw it in 1678, gave Europe its first description.
Some 275 cascades along a horseshoe of the Iguazu, named for great water in Guarani. Cabeza de Vaca came upon it in 1541.
The deepest and oldest lake on Earth, holding a fifth of the world's fresh surface water. Russian Cossacks under Kurbat Ivanov reached its shore in 1643.
A salt lake at the lowest point on land, so dense a swimmer floats. It figures in Genesis, and Aristotle had heard that nothing could sink in it.
A pyramid of rock and snow in western Tibet, sacred to Hindus, Buddhists, Jains and Bon. Pilgrims walk around it rather than climb it; no one has stood on its summit.
A volcanic island in the Sunda Strait. Its eruption in 1883 was heard nearly five thousand kilometres away, and telegraph cables carried the news around the world within hours.
Some two thousand limestone pillars rising from the Gulf of Tonkin. Its name, the bay of the descending dragon, comes from a legend of dragons spitting jewels to wall off invaders.
Africa's largest lake, known around its shores as Nalubaale and Nyanza. Speke reached it in 1858 and declared it the source of the Nile, a claim argued for twenty years.
The Blue Nile thunders out of Lake Tana into a gorge. The Jesuit Pedro Páez, who saw the source in 1618, was the first European to describe it; Bruce claimed the honour in 1770.
The highest peak in the Alps, long called the Accursed Mountain. Its first ascent, by Balmat and Paccard in 1786, is often taken as the birth of mountaineering.
A volcano on the Armenian highlands where tradition grounded Noah's ark. Friedrich Parrot first climbed it in 1829.
The most honoured of China's five sacred mountains. Emperors climbed it to report to Heaven, the First Emperor among them in 219 BCE.
A granite peak in the south of the Sinai, held to be where Moses received the law. St Catherine's Monastery has stood at its foot since the sixth century.
The world's highest waterfall, falling nearly a kilometre from the flat top of Auyán-tepui. The Pemón call it Kerepakupai Merú; outsiders learned of it from the pilot Jimmie Angel in 1933.
Rome's frontier across northern Britain, eighty Roman miles of stone with a fort every mile. Abandoned when the legions left; Bede described it, and Camden made it famous again in 1586.

The longest waterway people ever dug, carrying the grain of the south to the capitals of the north. It was cut and recut for two thousand years, each age along its own course as the capitals moved; the map follows the route of the age.

phases.name: Early canals
phases.note: The king of Wu cuts the Hangou from the Yangtze to the Huai in 486 BCE; the Honggou soon links the Yellow River to the Huai's tributaries.

phases.name: Sui and Tang
phases.note: Sui joins the old canals into one system in six years: the Tongji from Luoyang to the Huai, the Yongji north to Zhuojun, and the canal south to Hangzhou. Tang feeds its capitals with it.

phases.name: Northern Song
phases.note: The Bian canal brings the grain of the south to Kaifeng, the largest city in the world; the northern branch has silted up.

phases.name: Southern Song
phases.note: The Jin take the north and the Yellow River floods across the Bian; only the canal south of the Yangtze still serves, to the new capital at Hangzhou.

phases.name: Yuan
phases.note: The Mongols cut a straight new course through Shandong to Dadu, the Beijing of today, bypassing Luoyang and Kaifeng; much grain still goes by sea.

phases.name: Ming and Qing
phases.note: Ming reopens the canal in 1411 and from 1604 routes it clear of the Yellow River; for four centuries it carries the grain tribute to Beijing.

phases.name: After 1855
phases.note: The Yellow River swings north and cuts the canal in Shandong; the grain goes by sea and rail, and only the southern reaches stay in use.

story: A great passage tomb older than the pyramids, its passage lit by the rising sun at midwinter. In Irish tradition it was Brú na Bóinne, home of the Dagda; antiquaries found its entrance in 1699.
Some three thousand standing stones in long rows across the Breton heath, raised by the first farmers of the Atlantic coast. Local legend held they were a Roman legion turned to stone.
An abbey on a tidal island, cut off from the land twice a day. Pilgrims crossed the sands to it for centuries; it appears on the Bayeux Tapestry.
A cave painted with horses, aurochs and stags some seventeen thousand years ago. Four teenagers following their dog found it in 1940.
A cave ceiling of bison painted in red and black. A girl looked up and saw them in 1879; for twenty years experts refused to believe anything so fine could be prehistoric.
A Buddha seventy-one metres tall carved from the cliff where three rivers meet, to calm the waters for boatmen. It took ninety years to finish.
Two great Buddhas cut into a cliff on the road between India and Central Asia; Xuanzang saw them gilded in 630. They stood fourteen centuries until they were blown up in 2001.

Darius's account of his rise, carved high on a cliff in Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian. Rawlinson copied it hanging from ropes, and it unlocked cuneiform as the Rosetta Stone unlocked hieroglyphs.
A quarter-mile earthwork in the shape of an uncoiling serpent on an Ohio ridge. Who built it, and when, is still argued; Squier and Davis surveyed it in 1846.
The great stupa raised by Ashoka and ringed by carved gateways telling the Buddha's lives. Forgotten as Buddhism faded in India, it was found overgrown by a British officer in 1818.
The largest structure made by living things, two thousand kilometres of coral off Queensland. Cook ran aground on it in 1770 and spent weeks repairing the Endeavour.
A pyramid of rock on the Swiss–Italian border. Whymper's party reached its summit in 1865; four of them fell to their deaths on the way down.
The highest mountain outside Asia. Inca priests climbed high on it to make offerings; a Swiss guide first reached the summit in 1897.
The smoking mountain that watches over the Valley of Mexico. Cortés's men climbed it in 1519 to gather sulphur for gunpowder.
An ice-capped volcano long thought the highest mountain on Earth. Humboldt climbed higher on it in 1802 than anyone had been, and drew his famous chart of plants by altitude.
The highest peak in North America, the High One to the Koyukon. Vancouver saw it from the sea in 1794; it was first climbed in 1913.
Geysers, boiling springs and painted canyons over a slumbering supervolcano. John Colter's tales of it in 1807 were laughed at; in 1872 it became the world's first national park.
A river that never reaches the sea, spreading into a vast green delta in the Kalahari. Livingstone crossed its edge on the way to Lake Ngami in 1849.
A volcano rising straight from the Gulf of Guinea. The Carthaginian Hanno saw it burning at night around 500 BCE and called it the Chariot of the Gods.
The highest peak of the Southern Alps, Aoraki to the Māori, a boy turned to stone. Tasman saw the great range in 1642; it was named for Cook in 1851.
One of the most active volcanoes on Earth, home of the fire goddess Pele. The missionary William Ellis described its lava lake in 1823.
Granite peaks rising from a sea of cloud, crooked pines on their ledges. Xu Xiake climbed them in 1616 and said that after Huangshan he need see no other mountain.
The highest mountain in Greece, home of the gods in Homer and Hesiod. No one is recorded climbing to its summit until 1913.
A limestone rock guarding the strait between the Mediterranean and the Ocean, one of the Pillars of Hercules. For the ancients it marked the end of the known world.
Some forty thousand basalt columns stepping into the sea, said to be the road of the giant Finn McCool. Reported to the Royal Society in 1693.
The highest great lake in the world, where the Inca said the sun and the first people rose from the water. Cieza de León described it in 1553.
A great shallow lake on the edge of the Sahara, heart of the empire of Kanem-Bornu. Denham, Clapperton and Oudney were the first Europeans to see it, in 1823.
A sandstone plateau of stone forests and painted shelters, its art recording a green Sahara of cattle, giraffes and swimmers. A French officer first reported the paintings in 1933.
The highest volcano in Eurasia, rising over Kamchatka. Cossacks under Atlasov saw it in 1697; Krasheninnikov described it for the Russian Academy.
The hot spring that gave every geyser its name, shooting water high into the Icelandic air. Icelanders recorded its eruptions from 1294.
Norway's longest and deepest fjord, two hundred kilometres into the mountains. Viking fleets sailed from its shores; Romantic painters made it famous in the nineteenth century.
Europe's highest active volcano, the forge of Hephaestus. The philosopher Empedocles was said to have leapt into its crater.
A valley of soft volcanic rock worn into cones and chimneys, carved within into churches and whole underground towns. The traveller Paul Lucas described its strange pinnacles in 1705.
Four hills rising from the Kalahari, painted with thousands of images; to the San, where the first spirit knelt to pray after creating the world.
The southernmost active volcano, smoking over the Ross Sea. James Clark Ross named it for his ship in 1841; Shackleton's men first climbed it in 1908.
Monasteries built on top of sandstone pillars in Thessaly, reached for centuries by ladders and nets hauled up by rope.
Temples of the Chandela kings carved with thousands of figures of gods, dancers and lovers; overgrown when the dynasty fell, they were shown to a British officer in 1838.
A temple to the sun god built as a giant stone chariot with twenty-four carved wheels. Its tower, a landmark for ships in the Bay of Bengal, was known to sailors as the Black Pagoda.
Thirty-four cave temples, Buddhist, Hindu and Jain side by side, among them the Kailasa temple, carved downward from a single mass of rock.
The great crusader castle of the Hospitallers in Syria, which held out for a century and a half until Baybars took it in 1271.
A fortified village of earthen houses on the caravan route from the Sahara to Marrakesh, over the High Atlas.
The walled citadel of the Chachapoya, the Cloud Warriors, on a ridge above the Utcubamba, with walls up to nineteen metres high; forgotten after the Spanish conquest until 1843.
A wall of concrete across the Colorado, built in five years in the Depression, which made Lake Mead and lit the cities of the American South-west.
The largest power station ever built, damming the Yangtze above Yichang; its reservoir drowned towns and temples for six hundred kilometres upstream.
Herod's palace-fortress on a cliff above the Dead Sea, where Jewish rebels held out against Rome until 73 or 74 CE.
One of the first towns, a honeycomb of mud-brick houses entered through the roof, painted with bulls and hunters nine thousand years ago.
The great gilded stupa of Yangon, said to hold eight hairs of the Buddha; the English merchant Ralph Fitch described it in 1586.
The Roman temples of Heliopolis in the Beqaa valley, built on foundation stones weighing up to a thousand tonnes.
A walled hill town with fifty-two towers, besieged in the Albigensian Crusade and rebuilt, rather freely, by Viollet-le-Duc from 1853.
The highest mountain on Earth, Chomolungma to the Tibetans. Measured as Peak XV by the Survey of India in 1852–56 and named for its former head; first climbed in 1953.
Snow-capped mountains on the equator: Ptolemy's Mountains of the Moon, where he placed the source of the Nile. Stanley saw them in 1888.
A broken volcanic peak on the equator, Kirinyaga, the seat of God, to the Kikuyu. The missionary Krapf saw its snows in 1849.
The largest unbroken caldera on Earth, a crater twenty kilometres across full of grazing herds, the land of the Maasai.
The longest freshwater lake in the world, reached by the caravan trade from the Swahili coast at Ujiji; Burton and Speke arrived in 1858.
The highest mountain of Borneo, held by the Kadazan to be the resting place of the dead; Hugh Low climbed it in 1851.
A volcano on Sumbawa whose eruption in 1815, the largest in recorded history, darkened the skies of the world and brought the year without a summer.
A volcano on the border of Korea and Manchuria with a crater lake at its summit, sacred to Koreans and to the Manchu; its eruption around 946 was among the greatest of the last two thousand years.
Once the fourth largest lake in the world, between the deserts of Central Asia. Its rivers were diverted to water cotton from the 1960s, and most of it has dried away.
A volcano that has erupted every few minutes for thousands of years, the lighthouse of the Mediterranean; to the Greeks, the home of Aeolus, keeper of the winds.
A ring of islands around a drowned caldera. Its eruption around 1600 BCE buried the Bronze Age town of Akrotiri under ash.
A marble peak at the end of a peninsula, where Xerxes cut a canal to spare his fleet its storms; a republic of monasteries since the tenth century.
A granite valley in the Sierra Nevada, home of the Ahwahneechee; a militia chasing them entered it in 1851, and in 1864 it was set aside for the public.
The small lake where the Mississippi begins, found in 1832 by Henry Schoolcraft with the Ojibwe guide Ozawindib.
The largest salt flat on Earth, a white plain on the Bolivian altiplano where a prehistoric lake dried away.
A fjord between sheer granite walls in the south-west of New Zealand, Piopiotahi to the Māori.

A cliff at the northern end of Europe. The Norse chieftain Ohthere sailed round it about 890 and told King Alfred of the voyage; the English captain Richard Chancellor named it in 1553, looking for a way to China.
The oldest desert on Earth, where red dunes three hundred metres high run down to the Atlantic.
Thousands of sandstone pillars rising from the forest of western Hunan, made a national park in 1982.
Three granite towers at the edge of the Patagonian ice field.
The palace-fortress of the Nasrid sultans, the last Muslim rulers of Spain, its courts of water and carved stucco handed over to Ferdinand and Isabella in 1492.
The Flavian amphitheatre, which held some fifty thousand spectators for games and executions. After the last games in 523 it became a quarry, a fortress and finally a monument.
The temple of Athena on the Acropolis. It stood almost whole as a church and then a mosque for two thousand years, until a Venetian shell blew up the powder stored inside in 1687.
Justinian's church of Holy Wisdom, whose dome seemed to hang from heaven; the largest church in the world for a thousand years, a mosque from 1453, a museum from 1934 and a mosque again from 2020.
The golden dome over the rock from which, in Islamic tradition, Muhammad ascended to heaven, on the site of the Jewish Temple; the oldest surviving great Islamic building.
The great mosque of Umayyad Córdoba, a forest of more than eight hundred columns under red and white arches; a cathedral was built in its middle in the sixteenth century.
The fortress of Moscow's princes on a hill above the river, rebuilt in red brick by Italian masters in the 1480s and 1490s, with the cathedrals where the tsars were crowned.
An iron tower three hundred metres high, built for the Exposition of 1889 and meant to stand for twenty years; the tallest structure in the world until 1930.

The largest religious monument in the world, built by Suryavarman II as a temple to Vishnu. When Angkor was abandoned it stayed a Buddhist monastery; a Portuguese friar described it in 1586, and Mouhot's account made it famous in 1860.
The palace of the Ming and Qing emperors, nearly a thousand buildings within purple walls, closed to all but the court; Matteo Ricci entered it in 1601.
Where the emperor prayed each winter for good harvests, its round hall roofed in blue tiles for the sky.
The palace of the Dalai Lamas, rising thirteen storeys up the Red Hill. Two Jesuits sketched it in 1661; photographs reached the world after the British invasion of 1904.
The great temple of Nara, whose Great Buddha Hall, rebuilt in 1709, was long the largest wooden building in the world.
The tomb Shah Jahan built for his wife Mumtaz Mahal in white marble on the Yamuna; the French traveller Bernier described it in 1663.
A copper colossus given by France, holding a torch over New York harbour; for millions of emigrants the first sight of America.
Shah Abbas's great square, half a kilometre long, framed by the royal mosque, the palace and the bazaar; Isfahan, the Persians said, is half the world.
Three madrasas facing one another across Samarkand's central square, the first built by Ulugh Beg, the astronomer prince.

The great shallow lake of the Valley of Mexico, with Tenochtitlan on an island in its western arm, joined to the shore by causeways. Drained from 1607 to stop the city flooding, it was all but gone by 1900.
The salt lake at the end of the Tarim, beside ancient Loulan, which seemed to wander across the desert as the river shifted. Hedin mapped it in 1901; once the Tarim was dammed, it dried up in 1972.
